response.query: Which IRT and multi-group CFA strategies most reliably detect differential item functioning in digital-literacy and social-capital scales across SES and rural/urban groups?
response.answer: Multi-group IRT and generalized Mantel-Haenszel statistics reliably detect differential item functioning across SES and rural/urban groups. These methods compare item parameters and detect bias in digital-literacy and social-capital scales.

results.title: Differential Item Functioning (DIF): Complete Guide to Test Fairness | Cogn-IQ
results.content: # Differential Item Functioning (DIF). Differential Item Functioning (DIF) occurs when test items perform differently for subgroups of equal ability, potentially indicating test bias. DIF analysis identifies items that unfairly advantage or disadvantage specific demographic groups, ensuring test fairness and validity across diverse populations. Differential Item Functioning (DIF) is a statistical property of test items that occurs when individuals from different groups (such as gender, ethnicity, or language background) with the same underlying ability level have different probabilities of answering an item correctly. DIF provides a framework for identifying and addressing such bias at the item level, distinguishing it from legitimate group differences in the construct being measured. * Understand the distinction between DIF and item bias. * Learn major statistical methods for DIF detection. * Recognize the implications of DIF for test validity and fairness. Uniform DIF occurs when the performance difference between groups remains constant across all ability levels. For example, if an item consistently favors one group by the same amount regardless of ability level, it exhibits uniform DIF. Non-uniform DIF occurs when the performance difference between groups varies across ability levels. This method can detect both uniform and non-uniform DIF through hierarchical model comparison. IRT-based DIF detection compares item parameters across groups, examining differences in difficulty, discrimination, and guessing parameters. This approach addresses the contamination problem where DIF items affect the matching variable, providing more accurate detection especially when multiple items exhibit DIF. When examining DIF across multiple groups simultaneously, methods include generalized Mantel-Haenszel statistics, multiple indicator multiple cause (MIMIC) models, and multi-group IRT approaches. Bundle DIF examines differential functioning at the testlet or subscale level rather than individual items. Bundle DIF can reveal systematic bias patterns that individual item analysis might miss. DIF analysis informs item writing and revision processes. Items flagged for DIF undergo content review to identify potential sources of bias, such as culturally specific references, gendered language, or differential curricular exposure. DIF analysis provides empirical evidence for test fairness, supporting legal defensibility under employment and educational testing guidelines. In international testing programs, DIF analysis identifies items that function differently across countries or languages. A handbook on the theory and methods of differential item functioning (DIF).

results.title: Full article: Item Response Theory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis: Complementary Approaches for Scale Development
results.content: This article demonstrates the advantages of using both confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and item response theory (IRT) in the development and evaluation of social work scales with dichotomous or polytomous items. Complementary CFA and IRT results provide detailed information about item and scale performance of the social isolation scale. Researchers conducting CFAs can choose among estimation options based on the measurement level and distributional characteristics of observed variables – an important feature given that the majority of scales used in social work research and practice have items with dichotomous or ordinal response options that do not meet normality assumptions. These attributes include item and scale information, conditional standard errors, conditional reliability, model-based person scores in both the θ metric and transformed estimated true scores, differential item functioning, and differential scale functioning. Further, our IRT analysis found that each item substantively contributed to scale information, conditional standard errors, and conditional reliability, all of which indicated the scale operated with most precision in the 0 ≤ θ ≤ +2 range (see , #11). Loadings and slopes, thresholds and location parameters can be evaluated at both the item and scale levels (through measurement invariance and multiple group analysis in CFA, differential item, and test analysis in IRT). If the goal of the ESSP scale is to provide an assessment of the full range of the social isolation construct, implications of the IRT analysis would be that items measuring lower levels of social isolation should be identified and tested. (Scale items supported in a factor analysis are often subsequently subjected to an internal consistency reliability test to further support their collective use.) We should note, however, that examination of item thresholds obtained in the CFA analysis also provided insights into the range of the social isolation construct captured with items and corroborated the findings from the IRT analysis. Both CFA factor loadings and IRT slope parameters indicated items were responsive to differences in levels of the latent construct or θ. By adding items designed to measure lower levels of social isolation, we improve both construct representation (validity) and extend scale information, conditional standard errors, and conditional reliability across a broader range of θ.

results.title: Differential Item Functioning - IQ Test
results.content: Differential Item Functioning (DIF) in Cognitive Testing. Differential Item Functioning (DIF) occurs when individuals from different groups (e.g., genders, races, or ethnicities) with the same underlying ability level have a different probability of answering a test item correctly or endorsing a particular response. DIF is an important concept in cognitive testing and educational measurement, where ensuring fairness and validity across diverse populations is essential. DIF analysis is used to detect items on a test that may be biased or function differently for one group compared to another. An item exhibits DIF when test-takers with the same ability, but from different groups, do not have an equal chance of selecting the correct answer or giving a particular response. Ensuring that cognitive tests are free from DIF is crucial as these assessments are used to make important decisions about education, employment, and psychological evaluation. Differential Item Functioning is a vital aspect of cognitive test development and analysis, aimed at detecting bias and ensuring that test items are appropriate and equitable for all examinees.
